newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Duma set to debate 1997 budget on Sunday.
newsitem.headline: Russian Duma set to debate 1997 budget on Sunday.

text.p: Russian parliament is due to debate the 1997 budget on Sunday, but it remains unclear if legislators, who have deeply divided views on how much the government should spend, will finally approve the plans.
The Communist-dominated State Duma, or lower house of parliament, has rejected the government's ideas once and postponed a vote on a second occasion.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Tuesday he hoped the draft would be passed this time.
"We will continue discussing the budget on December 15 and I hope we will get it approved," he told the upper house of parliament.
"We have to adopt the budget because the country cannot live in the first quarter of next year under the budget for the fourth quarter of 1996... We cannot allow that."
Russian markets were closed on Thursday and Friday, but this coming Sunday is a working day in Russia.

If deputies fail to approve a budget by the end of the year, Russia will have to use interim budgets or stick with the 1996 plan. The Duma, after a long day of heated debate, last Friday delayed discussion of a rejigged draft until December 15.

Apart from the potentially chaotic effect on the day-to-day running of the economy of not having a budget, a delay in passing the draft could further jeopardise monthly payouts of Russia's $10 billion International Monetary Fund (IMF) loan.
The IMF has twice delayed handing over tranches of the loan because of worries about low tax revenues. The IMF board meets on Friday to decide whether to release a new tranche.
Mikhail Zadornov, chairman of the Duma's budget committee, said on Tuesday he believed the draft would be passed on Sunday.
But Boris Nemtsov, the liberal governor of the industrial Nizhny Novgorod region, said in London that political factors could prevent the budget being passed.
"I'm not sure the budget will be adopted next week," he said. "Not because it's bad but because of political problems."
The draft foresees a deficit of 3.5 percent of gross domestic product and Chernomyrdin told the upper house this was "the maximum permissible figure".
The Russian government has championed a tight monetary policy which has led to steep falls in monthly inflation, from close to 20 percent in January 1995 to 1.9 percent in November.
But the squeeze has also contributed to misery for millions of workers, who have not been paid for months by cash-strapped firms. Tax revenue, in turn, is well below target.

Chernomyrdin said that if budget targets were met and 1997 annual inflation did not exceed 11-12 percent, the economy could grow by two percent. GDP fell six percent in real terms in the first 10 months of the year from the January-October period last year.
The draft deficit has been widened from the government's initial proposal of 3.3 percent and Chernomyrdin said anything more could be damaging.
"We must not allow this to happen. If we do, all our sufferings and pains will be in vain," he said.
But communist deputies, who make up the largest faction in the Duma want more spending -- to be covered by printing money.

Budget problems have cast a cloud over an economy which the government is keen to integrate with the international mainstream. Russia marked its Euromarket debut with a heavily oversubscribed $1 billion issue last month.
The upper house increased pressure on Chernomyrdin on Tuesday, saying the government was not up to the task of tackling the country's problems.
Chernomyrdin had earlier pledged to pay off wage and pension arrears. Russian leaders have made similar promises throughout the year.
